title: Prisoner not responsive, couldn't walk at hand-over, court hears
subtitle: Debra Chrisjohn didn't respond to questions and couldn't walk to a nearby police cruiser when London police Const. Nicholas Doering handed her over to two Elgin County OPP officers hours before she died, an OPP officer testified Tuesday.
article: Debra Chrisjohn didn't respond to questions and couldn't walk to a nearby police cruiser when London police Const. Nicholas Doering handed her over to two Elgin County OPP officers hours before she died, an OPP officer testified Tuesday.

Doering - who is charged with criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life in Chrisjohn's Sept. 7, 2016, death while in custody - said she had been medically cleared during the handover, OPP Const. Ashleigh Billing told the court.
"My understanding is that she'd been assessed and did not require hospitalization," Billing said.

Chrisjohn, 39, had been arrested a few hours earlier after she was seen walking into traffic near the intersection of Highbury Avenue and Trafalgar Street in London. She was transferred to Elgin OPP on an outstanding warrant for breaching a recognizance. She died later in the St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital.
Billing and OPP Const. Mark McKillop met Doering in the Tim Hortons parking lot at Highbury Avenue to pick up Chrisjohn.

Chrisjohn, an Oneida Nation of the Thames resident and mother to 11, was lying in the backseat of Doering's cruiser handcuffed, shaking and moaning, said Billing, who explained to her why she was being taken into custody.
"I am talking to her, telling her every step that we're doing so there's no surprises, but she doesn't say anything back to me," Billing told the court.
Billing and McKillop removed Chrisjohn from the backseat of the cruiser and helped her to their vehicle after she was frisked, said Billing, who will continue to testify Wednesday.

In July 2017, Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, charged both Doering and McKillop in Chrisjohn's death, but the Crown withdrew the charges against McKillop five months later.
More than a dozen uniformed officers have attended the first two days of the trial to support Doering, who has been assigned to administrative duties since being charged.
Earlier in the day, the court heard from two London paramedics who responded to the call where Chrisjohn was arrested.
The call came in for a woman having a panic attack after a woman who was "high on drugs" tried to get into her minivan with her child inside, the court heard.
Paramedic Sean Hill, a supervisor for Elgin Middlesex EMS, described seeing Chrisjohn in the back of Doering's cruiser when he arrived at the scene.
"She was acting aggressively, throwing herself against the passenger side door and yelling profanities," he said, noting the woman was conscious and didn't appear to have any trouble breathing.
Neither Hill, who testified he thought Chrisjohn was the woman for whom he was called to treat, or the other two responding paramedics - Sarah May and Devon Mason - did an assessment of Chrisjohn.

Defence lawyer Lucas O'Hara grilled Hill and May, who also took the stand Tuesday, highlighting inconsistencies between the incident reports they filed and interviews they gave to investigators from the Ministry of Health and the SIU.
Hill had told his supervisor he'd offered to assess Chrisjohn, but he testified he hadn't made the offer, the court heard.
"You lied to your boss because you didn't want any negative findings against you," O'Hara said.
Hill denied the assertion, but conceded there was "some misinformation."
The trial is scheduled to continue until Tuesday.
